comments.author: Almaravarion
comments.body:
Vibecoding? Yes. Will it be good? Not a snowflake's chance in hell; At least not for now.

AI Assisted Development however, with multiple design passes, revisions, testing, etc. where the LLMs take care of the code are possible.

The problem here is that to make something good, with or without AI, You still need some competence, knowledge and skill; AI pushes the skill focus away from hard code a bit, though there are countless small details that make or break games, that AI will not catch, simply due to lack of knowledge and e.g. haptic experience. 

For example - on paper making a thermometer with small numbers on it sound good and realistic, but if You take into account how the user interacts with it, user/tester would realize that numbers are completely or functionally unreadable most of the time.

replies.author: MrNotmark
replies.body:
Maybe you can do it without understanding it sure. If you're working alone it matters less as well since you don't have to worry someone breaking your code (if the AI truly becomes pitch perfect it will also not break your code sure)

But will it be a massive advantage that you understand how it works? Absolutely.
I'm a professional software dev, I can see immediately who uses AI without understanding the code and who uses AI as an assist tool.
Even just coming up with ideas, when you have deep knowledge and you understand the systems it will be significantly easier when you actually understand how they work and what they can do and what are the limitations.
A simple game sure you can do it with AI any day, but will you also outsource the thinking part to AI as well? Or do you actually want to be the one making decisions or will you let the AI give you the options and you just press Tab?
Ai might do what you asked for, but maybe it will do it literally exactly how you asked, and maybe that one will give you massive headaches later on. And you won't understand why. You will send the AI to hunt for bugs but will you let AI decide where the bugs are?
And it might find all of them eventually. It might take you a month with who knows how many tokens. When a simple common sense would've helped you find it in 2 days.
If you think AI can do the thinking for you good luck

replies.author: Almaravarion
replies.body:
Effectively Vibecoding is what I'd describe as someone deciding 'You know what, I have a vibe to make a strategy game', then goes to AI model, and writes something along the lines of 'You know what, make me a strategy game; Today I feel like playing something like age of empires, but there was no weather; let's add that', and effectively wait for LLM to deal its magic.

Key parts here are that design is optional, and the intent is based on vibes, rather than actually thought out development process.

Contrast to it AI assisted development, where for example, user starts with describing the overall concept, then refines it through e.g. adversarial process of main concept, and then designs a framework for each and every step on the way. Then, even if the implementation is done by LLM mostly by itself, every once in a while (due to technical limitations and nuances I'd recommend more often than more rarely), they test, adjust, iterate, until the product is made. 

While the former may take few hours to days to process the request, the latter usually starts with weeks for simpler implementations.

  
This is simplified description, but gives core of the difference across (hopefully).

replies.author: darkoblivion000
replies.body:
People’s wording and how they think about things is different from person to person. Think about it this way; someone who puts in a lot of thought and effort into a game, planning, balancing, polishing, can make a successful game. Someone who is just in it for “can ai make me a game that I can use to make money?” Is probably not going to put in the effort to do all that.

The casual way in which the post was worded makes it seem like OP just has the idea to make money off ai making a game. That’s why many of these responses are somewhat negative. Someone who comes in thinking “I can use ai to make money in gaming” is not going to succeed.

In this particular comment I agree with you. They probably meant vibe coding as in “Claude make me a game. Ok now add this. Ok now add this” with not much thought as to game design, how to make a game fun, how to build a good user interface. 

If you are acting as a game director and using AI to write the code but in other game design and artistic direction are still designing the game and putting in the time and polish, then I think you can succeed in building a good game

replies.author: phantomimp
replies.body:
First you will lose money: AI subscriptions, Steam Fees, Assets costs, marketing, maybe playtesters etc. ... 

If you make a too simple game, it will get reverse engineered and posted as a copycat by somebody else.

You need to make a really fun, unique game that is not easy to copy. 

If your game uses AI assets, it will be called slop by the anti AI crowd.

Even if you do everything right and make a great game, you might still not make any money because it is not visible in the flood of new game releases.

View it as a fun hobby that might make you some money someday, but don't expect it to become your (main) income source.

I will ask claude for a high level summary of my project timeline and see what it says.

replies.author: jdheffa
replies.body:
Here it is again with the game specifics taken out:

| Dates | Focus |
|---|---|
| **Sep 13–16** | **Design and planning.** The core game design was written and its open questions were settled. Very little code. |
| **Sep 17–20** | **Art pipeline setup.** The tools and workflows for making art were built, and the first major art production began. |
| **Sep 21–24** | **Art.** Steady production with review and revision rounds. |
| **Sep 25–28** | **Art wrap-up, then coding.** The first milestone was finished and core gameplay coding began. |
| **Sep 29–Oct 2** | **Coding and art together.** Features and their look were built side by side. Bug fixing from playtests started. |
| **Oct 3–6** | **A major milestone.** Planning and building a large new layer of the game, with matching art and UI work. |
| **Oct 7–10** | **Audio and content.** The music was made and many features were built, some of them while you were away. Outside playtest feedback led to a refinement pass. |
| **Oct 11–14** | **Refactor, the busiest stretch.** A large cleanup run in parallel, covering testing tools, performance and bug fixes. A release process was set up. |
| **Oct 15–18** | **Polish and redesign.** Playtest fixes, plus a planned rework of one core system. |
| **Oct 19–22** | **New workflows.** The rework was finished and a daily art loop began. AI-generation tools were tried out and new features were added. |
| **Oct 23–25** | **Content and polish.** Daily art output went into the game, along with new features and a round of UI improvements. |

**The overall arc:** design first, then art tooling, then coding milestone by milestone. A big refactor came in the middle. Since then the work has been steady refinement driven by playtests, with art on a daily loop.

comments.author: J0rdian
comments.body:
If your goal is money then it's very unlikely, games industry for indies isn't really a good source of income. It's oversaturated because people do it as a hobby, for fun. And AI is making it even more common.

Also AI is insanely impressive for coding now a days but even if it does all the coding it's still not a game designer. It can make you a game, but it can't make it fun. So if you want to even try making a successful game you still have to be a good game designer, AI won't be able to help much there.

And this isn't even mentioning the art direction, assets, polish, juice. There are still aspects of making a game AI can't do super well.

So I will say this, making games is fun. And AI is lowering the barrier to entry. So I do recommend trying it if it sounds fun to you. Just again don't expect to be making profit.

comments.author: pvnimaxin
comments.body:
It depends. What kind of game are we talking about?

Making a game isn't just about coding. If you understand game development, then yes, it's possible. AI can handle a lot of the implementation these days, but knowing what to build and how to make it good is a different story.

Things like game design, art, sound design, storytelling, and animation can be challenging if you have no experience with them. An experienced animator will generally get much better results from AI animation tools than someone with no animation experience.

AI can help with all these things, but you still need to know what good looks like and how to evaluate the results. And of course, it depends heavily on the type and complexity of the game.
